# An In-Depth Review of *Middlemarch* by George Eliot

## "The History of Man's Condition": A Comprehensive Critical Analysis

---

## Preface: Why *Middlemarch* Demands Our Attention

There is a particular kind of novel that does not merely tell a story but constructs a world so complete, so morally and psychologically intricate, that the reader emerges from it changed — not in the dramatic, sudden way of a revelation, but in the slow, accumulative way of genuine experience. George Eliot's *Middlemarch: A Study of Provincial Life*, published in installments between 1871 and 1872, is precisely such a novel. Virginia Woolf called it "one of the few English novels written for grown-up people." Henry James, who was not given to easy praise, described it as "a treasure-house of detail, but... an indifferent whole" — a judgment that, while famously wrong about the whole, at least acknowledges the extraordinary richness of the parts. F.R. Leavis placed Eliot at the center of what he called "the great tradition" of English fiction. And yet, despite this chorus of critical admiration, *Middlemarch* remains, for many readers, an intimidating, even forbidding text — long, dense, philosophically demanding, and populated by characters whose inner lives are rendered with a precision that can feel almost uncomfortably intimate.

This review aims to do justice to that complexity. Over the course of this analysis, I will examine the novel's major themes — the nature of idealism and its collision with reality, the politics of marriage, the relationship between the individual and society, the question of what constitutes a meaningful life, the nature of sympathy and moral vision — as well as its narrative style, its use of irony, its structural architecture, its historical and biographical context, and its enduring relevance to contemporary readers. I will argue that *Middlemarch* is not merely a great Victorian novel but one of the most searching and honest accounts of human experience ever committed to prose — a book that earns its reputation not through the grandeur of its events but through the extraordinary depth of its attention to the ordinary.

---

## Part One: Context and Genesis

### George Eliot and the Making of *Middlemarch*

To understand *Middlemarch*, one must first understand something of the woman who wrote it. Mary Ann Evans — who published under the male pseudonym George Eliot to ensure her work was taken seriously in a literary culture that condescended to women writers — was one of the most intellectually formidable figures of the Victorian age. She had translated Strauss's *Das Leben Jesu* and Feuerbach's *Das Wesen des Christenthums*, works of German biblical criticism that had profoundly shaken her Christian faith and replaced it with what might be called a secular humanism — a belief in the moral importance of sympathy, fellow-feeling, and the recognition of other people's inner lives as real and valuable as one's own. She was deeply versed in philosophy, science, history, and music. She lived, scandalously for her time, with the philosopher and critic George Henry Lewes, who was legally unable to divorce his estranged wife, in a relationship that was by all accounts one of the great intellectual and emotional partnerships of the century.

This biographical context matters because *Middlemarch* is, among other things, a novel about the consequences of living in a society that does not accommodate the full range of human aspiration — particularly female aspiration. Eliot herself had found a way, through extraordinary intelligence, determination, and the support of Lewes, to live a life of intellectual and creative fulfillment. But she was acutely aware that most women of her era could not. The novel's famous Prelude, which invokes the figure of Saint Theresa of Ávila as a woman whose "unhistoric acts" shaped the world, is a meditation on this very problem: what happens to the Theresas who are born into a world that offers them no epic to participate in?

The novel itself grew from two separate projects. Eliot had begun a story about a young woman named Dorothea Brooke, and separately a story about a young doctor named Tertius Lydgate who comes to the provincial town of Middlemarch with ambitious plans for medical reform. At some point — and this is one of the great creative decisions in literary history — she recognized that these two stories belonged together, that their themes were deeply complementary, and that by weaving them into a single narrative she could create something far more powerful than either could be alone. The result is a novel with not one but several interlocking plots, each of which illuminates the others, and each of which explores, from a different angle, the same fundamental questions about human aspiration, social constraint, and the possibility of a meaningful life.

### The Historical Setting

*Middlemarch* is set in the years 1829-1832, a period of significant political and social upheaval in England. The Reform Act of 1832, which extended the franchise and redistributed parliamentary seats, was being hotly debated. The railways were beginning to transform the landscape and the economy. Medical science was in a period of rapid development, with new ideas about the causes of disease challenging established practice. The novel is thus set at a moment of transition — a moment when the old order was visibly crumbling and the new order had not yet fully emerged. This historical setting is not merely decorative; it is thematically essential. The characters of *Middlemarch* are all, in various ways, people who are trying to navigate a world in flux, people whose ambitions and ideals are shaped by — and often frustrated by — the particular historical moment in which they find themselves.

Eliot herself was writing from the vantage point of the 1870s, looking back at the 1830s with the benefit of hindsight. This temporal distance gives the novel a particular quality of retrospective irony — the narrator knows how things turned out, knows which reforms succeeded and which failed, knows which medical theories proved correct and which were abandoned. This knowledge inflects the narrative with a gentle but persistent awareness of the gap between human aspiration and historical outcome.

---

## Part Two: The Architecture of the Novel

### Structure and Plot

*Middlemarch* is divided into eight "books," each with a title that signals its thematic concerns: "Miss Brooke," "Old and Young," "Waiting for Death," "Three Love Problems," "The Dead Hand," "The Widow and the Wife," "Two Temptations," and "Sunset and Sunrise." This structure is not merely organizational; it reflects the novel's commitment to showing how individual lives intersect and influence one another in ways that the individuals themselves often cannot perceive.

The novel's four main plots are:

**The Dorothea-Casaubon-Ladislaw plot**: Dorothea Brooke, a young woman of passionate idealism and genuine intellectual hunger, marries the elderly scholar Edward Casaubon, believing that she can assist him in his great scholarly project — a "Key to All Mythologies" — and thereby participate in something larger than the domestic life that is all her society offers her. The marriage is a disaster. Casaubon is cold, pedantic, emotionally withholding, and — as Dorothea gradually and painfully discovers — intellectually bankrupt, his great project already superseded by German scholarship he has refused to engage with. After Casaubon's death, Dorothea falls in love with his young cousin Will Ladislaw, a relationship that Casaubon had tried to prevent from beyond the grave through a codicil to his will.

**The Lydgate-Rosamond plot**: Tertius Lydgate, a young doctor of genuine scientific talent and reforming ambition, comes to Middlemarch intending to pursue his medical research while practicing medicine. He becomes entangled with Rosamond Vincy, a beautiful, accomplished, and utterly self-absorbed young woman who has constructed an elaborate fantasy of what marriage to a gentleman-doctor will mean for her social position. Their marriage is another disaster, but of a different kind — not the disaster of disappointed intellectual aspiration but the disaster of two people who are fundamentally incompatible in their values and their understanding of what life is for.

**The Bulstrode plot**: Nicholas Bulstrode, the powerful banker and evangelical Christian who dominates much of Middlemarch's civic life, is revealed to have a dark past — he made his fortune through a business that dealt in stolen goods, and he suppressed information that would have allowed his first wife's daughter to inherit her mother's estate. When this past is exposed, Bulstrode is destroyed, and his destruction ripples outward to affect Lydgate, who has accepted money from him and is therefore tainted by association.

**The Fred Vincy-Mary Garth plot**: Fred Vincy, Rosamond's feckless but good-hearted brother, is in love with Mary Garth, the practical, clear-eyed daughter of the land agent Caleb Garth. Fred must prove himself worthy of Mary by abandoning his expectations of an inheritance and making something of himself through honest work. This plot is the most conventionally comic of the four, and it provides a kind of counterpoint to the tragic dimensions of the other stories.

These four plots are interwoven with extraordinary skill. Characters from one plot appear in others; events in one story have consequences in another; the same social world — the world of Middlemarch — contains and connects all of them. The effect is of a society rendered in three dimensions, a community in which no one's life is entirely separate from anyone else's.

### The Narrator

One of the most distinctive features of *Middlemarch* is its narrator — a presence that is at once authoritative and intimate, ironic and compassionate, omniscient and self-aware. The narrator of *Middlemarch* is not a neutral conduit for the story but an active, opinionated, philosophically engaged intelligence who comments on the action, reflects on the nature of human experience, and addresses the reader directly in a way that creates a sense of shared inquiry.

This narrator is, in many ways, the novel's most important character. It is the narrator who establishes the moral and philosophical framework within which the characters' lives are to be understood. It is the narrator who articulates the novel's central insights about sympathy, self-deception, and the nature of moral vision. And it is the narrator who, through the use of irony, maintains a critical distance from the characters even while entering into their inner lives with extraordinary empathy.

The narrator's irony is not the cold, detached irony of a satirist who holds his characters in contempt. It is, rather, a warm, compassionate irony — an irony that acknowledges human weakness and self-deception while refusing to condemn the people who exhibit them. When the narrator describes Casaubon's inner life — his fear of being found intellectually inadequate, his wounded pride, his genuine if limited capacity for feeling — we are invited to understand him even as we recognize his failures. When the narrator describes Rosamond's self-absorption, we are invited to see how it has been shaped by a society that has given her no outlet for her intelligence and energy except the cultivation of her own attractiveness. The irony, in other words, is always in the service of understanding.

---

## Part Three: Major Themes

### Theme One: Idealism and Its Discontents

The central drama of *Middlemarch* is the drama of idealism — of people who have large aspirations and who discover, through painful experience, that the world is not organized to accommodate those aspirations. This theme is announced in the novel's famous Prelude, which describes Saint Theresa as a woman who "found her epos in the reform of a religious order" and then asks what happens to those "later-born Theresas" who find "no coherent social faith and order which could perform the function of knowledge for the ardently willing soul."

Dorothea Brooke is the most obvious embodiment of this theme. She is a woman of genuine moral seriousness and intellectual hunger who is trapped in a world that offers her nothing to do with these qualities except marry well. Her marriage to Casaubon is an act of idealism — she genuinely believes that she can help him with his great work, that she can participate in something larger than herself. The tragedy of the marriage is not simply that Casaubon is a bad husband (though he is) but that Dorothea's idealism has led her to misread him entirely — to project onto him qualities he does not possess, to see in his pedantry a depth of learning that is not there.

But Lydgate's story is equally a story of idealism and its discontents. Lydgate comes to Middlemarch with a genuine scientific vision — he wants to discover the "primitive tissue" that underlies all organic life, to make a contribution to medical science that will matter. He is, in his professional life, a man of real intellectual distinction. But he is also a man who has never examined his assumptions about women and marriage, who has a "commonplace" view of women as ornamental creatures whose role is to provide a comfortable domestic background for the serious work of men. His marriage to Rosamond is the consequence of this unexamined assumption — he falls in love with her beauty and her social grace without ever asking whether she is a person he can actually live with.

The novel suggests that idealism, however genuine, is always in danger of becoming a form of self-deception — a way of seeing what we want to see rather than what is actually there. Dorothea's idealism leads her to misread Casaubon; Lydgate's idealism about his own scientific mission leads him to be careless about the rest of his life. The novel does not condemn idealism — it is clearly better to have large aspirations than small ones — but it insists that idealism must be accompanied by what the narrator calls "the growing good of the world": a willingness to see clearly, to acknowledge error, and to revise one's understanding in the light of experience.

### Theme Two: Marriage as Institution and Experience

*Middlemarch* is, among other things, one of the great novels about marriage — not marriage as a romantic ideal but marriage as a social institution and a lived experience. The novel presents us with several marriages, each of which illuminates a different aspect of the institution: the Dorothea-Casaubon marriage, the Lydgate-Rosamond marriage, the Bulstrode marriage, the Garth marriage, and eventually the Dorothea-Ladislaw and Fred-Mary marriages.

What is striking about Eliot's treatment of marriage is her refusal to sentimentalize it. The two central marriages of the novel — Dorothea-Casaubon and Lydgate-Rosamond — are both failures, and Eliot is unflinching in her analysis of why they fail. The Dorothea-Casaubon marriage fails because Dorothea has projected onto Casaubon qualities he does not possess, and because Casaubon is too wounded in his pride and too limited in his emotional capacity to meet Dorothea's need for genuine intellectual and emotional partnership. The Lydgate-Rosamond marriage fails because Lydgate has never taken Rosamond seriously as a person with her own desires and values, and because Rosamond is constitutionally incapable of subordinating her own wishes to anyone else's needs.

But Eliot is equally interested in what makes a marriage work. The Garth marriage — between Caleb Garth, the land agent who loves his work with a kind of religious devotion, and Susan Garth, his practical, intelligent wife — is presented as a model of what marriage can be when it is based on genuine mutual respect and shared values. The Garths are not wealthy; they are often financially precarious; but their marriage is a genuine partnership, and their home is a place of warmth and moral seriousness.

The novel's treatment of marriage is also deeply political. Eliot is acutely aware that marriage, in the Victorian era, was not merely a personal relationship but a legal and economic institution that gave men enormous power over women. Dorothea's situation after Casaubon's death — constrained by his codicil, dependent on his estate — illustrates this power with painful clarity. Rosamond's situation — trapped in a marriage she has come to resent, with no legal recourse and no economic independence — is equally illustrative. The novel does not make these points polemically; it makes them through the texture of lived experience, through the accumulation of small details that show how the institution of marriage shapes and constrains the lives of the people within it.

### Theme Three: The Individual and Society

One of the most persistent themes of *Middlemarch* is the relationship between the individual and the social world in which he or she lives. The novel's subtitle — "A Study of Provincial Life" — signals this concern: Eliot is interested not just in individual characters but in the social fabric that connects them, the web of relationships, obligations, gossip, and mutual dependence that constitutes a community.

The town of Middlemarch itself is a character in the novel — a collective entity with its own opinions, prejudices, and power dynamics. The town's opinion matters enormously to the characters who live in it. Lydgate's reputation is destroyed not by any legal judgment but by the court of public opinion, which decides that his association with Bulstrode makes him suspect. Dorothea's second marriage to Ladislaw is condemned by Middlemarch society as a betrayal of her class and her first husband's memory. The town's gossip, its social hierarchies, its networks of obligation and patronage — all of these are rendered with extraordinary precision and shown to have real consequences for the characters' lives.

But Eliot is not simply a social determinist. She believes in the possibility of individual moral agency — the possibility that people can, through effort and self-examination, resist the pressures of their social world and act according to their own best values.
